title: Nasdaq-100 Futures Fall 1.7% as Amazon and Intel Swoon After Earnings
excerpt: Futures pointed to a weak Friday open after Amazon fell up to 8% and Intel plunged up to 23% in extended trading, extending Thursday's tech sell-off.
body:
• Nasdaq-100 futures fell 1.5% to 1.7% after hours, with S&P 500 futures down 0.6% to 0.7%, as Amazon and Intel results disappointed.
  • Amazon fell about 6% to 8% in extended trading after a miss and negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion; Intel plunged 21% to 23% on a weak outlook.
  • Thursday's regular session already hurt: the Nasdaq fell 1.4%, the S&P 500 lost 0.3%, and Alphabet dropped about 13%, wiping out roughly $500 billion in market value.
  • Friday is October's final trading day, with the Nasdaq Composite on track for a 2.5% monthly decline against a 0.9% gain for the S&P 500.

Nasdaq-100 futures fell sharply on Thursday evening after earnings from Amazon and Intel missed expectations, extending a tech sell-off that had already cut 1.4% from the Nasdaq in regular trading. Futures tied to the Nasdaq-100 lost 1.5% to 1.7%, S&P 500 futures slid 0.6% to 0.7%, and Dow futures were little changed, according to Stocktwits and CNBC TV18 reporting carried by TradingView.

Amazon and Intel add to the pressure

Amazon shares fell about 6% to 8% in extended trading after third-quarter earnings and revenue fell short of Wall Street expectations. The company posted negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion, spent upwards of $77 billion on property and equipment in the quarter, and maintained its 2026 capital expenditure forecast at $220 billion. Its guidance midpoint also came in below analyst expectations, CNBC TV18 reported.

Intel fell harder. The chipmaker slid 21% to 23% after hours after issuing a weaker-than-expected fourth-quarter outlook, pointing to slumping personal computer demand and supply bottlenecks. Revenue in its client computing and physical artificial intelligence group declined 5% from a year earlier to $8.1 billion, even as total third-quarter revenue rose to $16.5 billion. Intel stock is still up 133% for the year after Thursday's close, which sharpened the after-hours drop.

"I think we're in a better, more stable place in October and heading into November in the tech trade than we were in August and September. But that said, I think investors are becoming much more selective."

— Art Hogan, Chief Market Strategist, B. Riley Wealth Management, to CNBC

A bad regular session came first

The futures move followed a weak day on Wall Street. The S&P 500 ended Thursday 0.3% lower at 7,720.39, the Nasdaq 100 fell 1.4% to 29,402.51, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average eased about 130 points to 52,342.56, while the small-cap Russell 2000 added 1%. Alphabet was the biggest drag, falling about 13% in its largest one-day drop on record and wiping out roughly $500 billion of market capitalisation after investors focused on its negative free cash flow. ServiceNow plunged 27%, its biggest fall on record, dragging software peers lower.

Semiconductor and technology funds reflected the same pressure: the VanEck and iShares semiconductor ETFs each fell about 1% on Thursday, and the Vanguard Information Technology ETF lost 1.1%. The US 10-year Treasury yield fell back to 4.93% from 5.05%, and Brent crude held around $115 a barrel.

The AI spending question

The common thread across Alphabet, Amazon and the broader sell-off is capital spending. Investors are asking whether the AI infrastructure buildout, now running at tens of billions of dollars per quarter per company, will convert into revenue fast enough to justify valuations. Amazon's cloud business performed well even as the headline numbers missed, which is why the reaction centred on cash flow and spending rather than demand. Our separate results coverage has the company-level detail for Amazon, Microsoft and Alphabet.

What to watch on Friday

Friday marks the final trading day of October. The Nasdaq Composite is poised for a 2.5% decline for the month, against a modest 0.9% advance for the S&P 500 and a 2.8% rise for the Dow. Whether the futures losses hold at the open will depend on whether buyers treat the Amazon and Intel drops as company-specific or as a verdict on the AI trade itself.
